Secunda: adaptive music demo

Walk through the valley with the arrow keys (or WASD, or the pad). When you enter the enemy camp, the game asks the model for combat music; when you leave it, for exploration music again.

Exploration
Tension
Combat Score

Secunda cannot generate in real time on a CPU, so the demo plays clips generated in advance. A GPU might make real-time generation possible, but this was not tested. The rule that picks the state is deliberately simple: it only checks whether the player is inside the enemy camp, as a stand-in for “an enemy is approaching”. A real game could compute the two controls from any part of its state, such as the distance to the enemies or the player's health. Each clip continues a few seconds of a Skyrim or Witcher 3 passage with the controls of its state; only the generated part is played, never the original music. Expect codec artefacts: the model predicts 8 EnCodec codebooks (6 kbps).

What the controls alone do, same prompt but different requests

Each row starts from the same second of a Slakh2100 (CC BY 4.0) test song and continues it three times with the same random numbers; only the requested controls change: low, high, or a step from low to high at 5 s (the experiment of Figure 1 in the report). The three songs were picked by a rule, not by ear: their measured change is the closest to the median of the 12 test prompts.
